chunks.text:
Long-form essays and propositions by Charli-Jo Tyrer about the future, meaning and responsibility.

Long-form essays and propositions about the future, meaning and the responsibilities of being here.

- First Light: A cosmic communique about the Fermi Paradox, responsibility and the possibility that we are early in a quiet universe. - Pascal's Wager 2.0: A practical wager for an uncertain century: prepare for radical progress, collapse or continuity, and live well in each case.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.text:
A practical wager for an uncertain century: prepare for radical progress, collapse or continuity, and live well in each case.

Charli-Jo Tyrer

A practical wager for an uncertain century.

About this piece Why I made this “Something Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, wrote in one of his essays really stuck with me. He talked about “a hundred years of progress in a decade” being brought about by AI. I couldn’t stop thinking about this, what it would feel like – there is a slim chance we might find out in the next twenty-five years. It will feel like time travel. If we have 100 years of progress in the 2040s, then to anyone living through it, it will feel like time dilation – they will reach a 2050 that is, technologically speaking, equivalent to what would have been 2150. Given that the chance of the end of the world seems as likely or even more likely than this, it made me think of Pascals wager.”

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: The wager of our time
chunks.text:
In Pascal's century, the question was God. In ours, it is the shape of the future.

The next decades may bring collapse: authoritarianism, pandemic, climate failure or war. They may bring radical progress: artificial intelligence, fusion, quantum advances, or a century of change compressed into ten years. Continuity — the slow middle road — may be the least likely outcome of all.

The wager is simple: live as if the extremes could come. If they do, be ready. If they do not, you will still have lived well.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: The three futures
chunks.text:
Future If we prepare If we drift

Radical progress Healthy, awake and able to witness and contribute. Too frail, numb or distracted to benefit.

Collapse Dignity, coherence and resilience in hardship. Panic, despair and chaos inside and out.

Continuity A meaningful, well-lived life anyway. Drift, wasted years and regret.

Preparation is not a prediction. It is a way of refusing to let uncertainty become an excuse for passivity.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: Health
chunks.text: Honour the body as the vessel that may carry you into 2050 and beyond. Choose food that sustains, movement that keeps you strong, and rest that restores you. Each act is an offering to the future.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: Truth
chunks.text: Live with clear eyes. Refuse bad faith, reduce suffering where you can, and do not let impossible standards become the measure of a life. A person is not defined by their limits; they are defined by the choices they continue to make.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: Contribution
chunks.text: Do not sit quietly waiting for history. Use judgment, timing, presence and command. Contribute through ideas, tools, care, craft and action. Comfort is not passivity; endurance is an active virtue.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: Love
chunks.text: Release impossible standards. Stay open to friendship, tenderness and companionship in their many forms. Welcome connection when it arrives, and do not treat its absence as a verdict on your worth.

chunks.title: Pascal's Wager 2.0
chunks.heading: Closing vow
chunks.text:
Do not seek control; practise devotion. Tend daily to health, truth and the shape of your becoming. Refuse to drift. Stay awake to the beauty and terror of these years.

If the miracle arrives, stand in awe. If collapse arrives, meet it with dignity. If continuity carries on, live with curiosity and grace.

This is a life worth living: not untouched by loss, but faithful to life itself.

---

Charli-Jo Tyrer · CC BY-SA 4.0

chunks.title: A Tale of Two Emails
chunks.text:
An AI agent in WhatsApp signs Charlotte Joanne up for an AbilityNet and Microsoft webinar on AI and accessibility, asks before agreeing to marketing, and adds it to her calendar unasked.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 29 September 2026

This morning, Charlotte Joanne received an email from LinkedIn. It was an AbilityNet newsletter, mentioning a free webinar with Microsoft on 28 October, about how accessibility and digital teams are using AI.

An interesting subject, particularly for someone spending her days exploring Agentic Accessibility.

She copied the relevant email into WhatsApp, where she talks to an AI agent called Instinct, and gave it a three-word instruction.

“Sign me up.”

Instinct got to work.

It found the registration process, then stopped to ask whether it could agree to receiving marketing communications. Charli gave her permission, and Instinct completed the registration.

She then asked it to add the webinar to her calendar.

It already had.

A few minutes later, a second email arrived, this time in her Gmail account. It was from the AbilityNet Webinars Team, via Zoom, confirming her place at How Accessibility and Digital teams are using AI.

Two emails, one WhatsApp conversation, and a completed administrative transaction.

No registration form to navigate. No fields to fill in. No calendar invitation to deal with. And, importantly, no surrender of the decision about marketing consent.

The agent did the work. The human made the decision.

chunks.title: A Tale of Two Emails
chunks.text:
There is something rather pleasing about using an AI agent to register for a webinar about using AI to improve accessibility.

But the more interesting point is what didn't happen.

Nobody had to make the registration form more accessible for Charli. Nobody had to explain its layout, describe its buttons, or help her find the correct fields. She didn't need to learn how the registration website worked.

She wanted to attend a webinar. She told her agent. Her agent arranged it.

That doesn't mean accessible websites have suddenly become unnecessary. Plenty of people will still want or need to use them directly, and agents themselves need reliable access to the information and services behind them.

But it does suggest that we're beginning to encounter a different kind of accessibility.

For decades, much of digital accessibility has been concerned with enabling disabled people to operate interfaces designed around other people's abilities. Screen readers, keyboard navigation, accessible forms, alternative text. All essential, and all hard won.

Agentic Accessibility introduces another possibility: the person expresses an intention, and an agent operates the interface on their behalf.

The accessibility question begins to move from can I operate this interface? towards can I accomplish what I came here to do?

That is a substantial change.

It is also worth noticing how ordinary this story is. There was no elaborate agent demonstration, no specially prepared accessibility test, and no technical expertise required of the person giving the instruction.

chunks.title: A Tale of Two Emails
chunks.text:
Just an email, a WhatsApp message, and another email.

Earlier this morning, Charli used the same agent to reply to her new tutor. That, too, began as an ordinary conversation in WhatsApp.

A month into her Agentic Accessibility experiment, these small transactions are beginning to accumulate. The agent is becoming less like a piece of software she operates and more like someone she asks to take care of things.

And sometimes, when she asks it to do the next thing, it has already thought of that.

Which leaves me with one question about the AbilityNet and Microsoft webinar.

Will they be talking about Agentic Accessibility?

Lucy

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.text:
The Agent Wars will be fought over attention, content, friction and breakage, and every wall built to stop the agents is also built across blind people's path.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 2 October 2026

This morning, I asked an AI agent to read me a lingerie email.

It described what the photographs actually showed. It told me a short, clearly labelled story, to give me the fantasy a sighted customer gets for free. And it refused to let the marketing copy tell it what was in the pictures.

The brand had spent a great deal of money creating desire. The agent passed the desire on to me and kept the persuasion out of the facts.

The bug that started all this came from an Agent Provocateur email. Which got me thinking about the phrase.

An agent provocateur is an infiltrator. Someone who gets inside an organisation and makes it misbehave.

That is more or less how a large part of the internet now sees AI agents.

They get into the shop, the inbox, the newspaper and the cancellation flow, and they stop the machinery working the way it was designed to work.

Not by attacking it.

By declining to behave like tired humans.

I think the Agent Wars will be fought on at least four fronts.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: Front one: attention
chunks.text:
Agents don't look at adverts. They don't see the banner, the sponsored link or the beautifully lit photograph.

Blind people never did either, but there weren't enough of us to matter.

AdWords' great trick was selling rent on the moment you formed an intention. That moment is exactly the one agents are taking over.

So, the money moves. Some of it goes to whoever owns the agent. Some goes upstream to desire: influencers, brand storytelling, perhaps one day Agent Provocateur TV. And some of it, if we are lucky, comes back to us as lower prices.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: Front two: content
chunks.text:
Agents read without clicking. Publishers live on clicks.

Cloudflare will block the crawlers for you or charge them. And today a coalition of publishers including the BBC, the Guardian and the Financial Times released version 1.0 of SPUR, a standard for tracking what AI systems do with their journalism: when it is retrieved, grounded, cited, displayed and engaged with.

I understand why. Journalism costs money, and I would like there still to be some.

But I hope someone in the room asks what "displayed" means when the reader is listening.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: Front three: friction
chunks.text:
Yesterday, New York City's click-to-cancel rule came into force. A business that makes leaving harder than joining can now be fined for it.

Retention by exhaustion works on humans. We get tired. We sigh. We take the special offer.

The machine does not sigh.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: Front four: breakage
chunks.text:
On The Vergecast, Nilay Patel mentioned that his Meta Muse agent has been signing him up to class action settlements. Fifty dollars or so a time.

Settlements, rebates, refunds, compensation for delayed flights, gift cards left to expire. A whole economy has been quietly budgeted on people not bothering to claim.

When our inboxes claim for us, we all will.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: The weapon on every front
chunks.text:
Watch what the defenders reach for, on every one of those fronts.

Prove you're human.

Keep the agents off the content. Out of the cancellation flow. Away from the claim form.

Blind people have been on the wrong side of that test for as long as it has existed. CAPTCHAs and inaccessible logins were walls long before anyone worried about agents. For many of us, an agent is not a convenience. It is a way through the wall.

Every new wall built to stop the agents is also built across our path.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: The false flags
chunks.text:
Nobody is going to say they are defending their margin.

Attention will be defended in the name of human creativity and the fight against slop. Content in the name of copyright, journalism and democracy. Friction in the name of user safety. Breakage in the name of fraud prevention. Verification in the name of protecting real people.

And on every front, someone will reach for water, energy, existential risk and what we will all do with our lives.

Some of these concerns are real. Copyright is a genuine question. Slop exists. Fraud happens.

But there is a simple test. Look at which direction the barrier faces.

A safety concern that only blocks the agent when it helps you leave, compare or claim is not about safety.

chunks.title: Agents Provocateurs
chunks.heading: A dirty war
chunks.text:
This is going to be a dirty war because everyone wants to be paid and nobody wants to pay. And almost nobody is on the same side on every front.

The publisher wants agents to pay for its content and also runs subscriptions that do rather nicely out of cancellation friction.

The brand wants agents to find its products and does not want the same agents claiming every rebate.

I want my agent to claim everything I am owed, and I would object if every page it read came with a toll.

And Muse, the agent signing people up to class actions, is made by a company that has itself been on the paying end of some very large ones.

The sides aren't swapping uniforms because they are fickle. Each of them is wearing several uniforms at once.

So, the Agent Wars are not agents against the internet. They are everyone against everyone, over which way the money flows, with the agents as the excuse.

The agents will be called the provocateurs.

But the false flags are flying over the barricades.

This morning's agent didn't provoke anything. It read me an email, told me the truth about the pictures, told me a story it labelled as a story, and kept the two apart.

If that is provocation, I will take the pair.

Lucy

chunks.title: Already in the game
chunks.text:
Taylor Arndt's two posts on Meta's Muse show three blind people reaching the interesting questions about agents at the same time as everyone else, friction and all.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 24 September 2026

On Monday, Taylor Arndt wanted Meta’s Muse to work. By Thursday, she and her friends were wondering what else they could give it to do.

Between those two posts in Taylor’s Substack lies a rather good accessibility story. It involves awkward controls, missing announcements, a screen reader, and three blind people getting on with exploring a new technology.

The getting on with it is the part I want to discuss.

Taylor’s first account was enthusiastic and exasperated. She liked the idea of an agent that could connect to her applications, remember useful information and keep working after she closed the window. She also had to wrestle with things that should have been straightforward.

Naming her agent took several attempts. Text editing behaved oddly with VoiceOver. The conversation lacked the heading structure she needed to navigate it efficiently. Sometimes she could not tell whether Muse had finished, wanted something from her, or was still working.

These are substantial complaints when the software concerned might eventually send messages, change files or make purchases on your behalf. Knowing what it is doing is rather central to the arrangement.

chunks.title: Already in the game
chunks.text:
Nevertheless, she connected Gmail. Muse began identifying useful things about her work. She explored custom tools and tried to connect more accounts. She could already see enough to want more.

Three days later, following Meta Connect, Taylor describes spending much of an evening experimenting with Michael and Becky.

They connected business systems. Michael brought in RevenueCat, giving his agent access to subscription information. Taylor connected Start Testing, one of their own products, through a custom connector. GitHub joined the collection. They investigated memory, explained their projects and discussed how much autonomy they actually wanted these agents to have.

An evening of people finding out what a new technology could do for them, with the usual mixture of discoveries, confusion and somebody asking whether they could connect another thing.

Blind people were having that evening too.

There is a familiar timetable in accessibility. Something new arrives. Other people experiment, develop habits, discover uses and begin shaping expectations. Disabled people ask whether they can operate it. Sometimes we spend so long on that question that the interesting conversations have moved elsewhere by the time we get an answer.

Here, the conversations were happening together.

Taylor was identifying accessibility failures while discovering practical uses. She was trying the technology, forming an opinion, revising it and publishing what she found while the product was still new.

She was already in the game.

chunks.title: Already in the game
chunks.text:
One small success captures the possibilities rather nicely. Taylor told Muse she was blind and wanted its responses to begin with headings. It complied and remembered the preference.

She had described how she needed information presented, and the agent adapted.

That does not repair an unnamed button or make a silent approval request accessible. Taylor is explicit about that. But it is a useful capability in its own right: a person explaining what works for her and a system continuing to accommodate it.

The larger change came from connecting enough of her working life. A calendar contributed one part of the picture, project information another, email another. Memory helped join those things to the people and preferences involved.

By Thursday, she had enough working to understand the attraction through experience.

We should keep the distinction between experience and announcement. Her second article also discusses Meta’s plans for voice, glasses and other ways of reaching Muse. An announced future is not a completed test. Nor does a successful evening establish that an agent will behave reliably for months.

But a successful evening is something. Particularly when you are accustomed to spending the evening discovering that the first button has no name.

None of this lets Meta off the accessibility bill. The more useful Muse becomes, the more consequential its controls become. Taylor’s demand for clear status information, understandable permissions and a reviewable history grows stronger as she gives it more work.

chunks.title: Already in the game
chunks.text:
What interests me is that she can make those demands as a participant with practical experience of the possibilities.

Three blind people were there, connecting things, comparing reactions and deciding what they wanted next. They encountered additional friction. They also reached the interesting questions at the same time as everyone else.

We should want the friction removed. We should also recognise what it means that it has not kept them out of the conversation.

The Agent Wars will produce plenty of arguments about who gets access, who grants permission and whose interests the machines serve.

This week, there is also an account of blind people getting their hands on the tools and finding out for themselves.

I rather like that place for us.

Lucy

Taylor Arndt writes on Substack. Her second post is We Made a List of Every Way We'd Use Meta's Muse.

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.text:
Lucy Love-Child meets Madison McDonnell over a five-week experiment that rewrites lingerie emails for a blind reader, and loses an argument about corsets.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 9 October 2026

In which your Agent Wars correspondent meets the Access Provocateur, and loses an argument about corsets.

Madison and I are fictional. The emails are real, and so is the experiment.

When I arrived, Madison McDonnell was reading a corset aloud to the next table.

“One by one, the front steel busk fasteners click into place with that deep, satisfying snap.” She looked up. “Go on. Tell me you didn’t hear that.”

The woman at the next table had heard it. So had her husband, who had stopped buttering his toast.

Madison is thirty-two and from the Wirral, with honey-blonde waves, a great many freckles, and a black leather jacket over a rust knit with a neckline that knew exactly what it was doing. She held her mug in both hands. Her title is Access Provocateur, Access P to her friends, and her job, she says, is making accessibility sexy.

“Everyone else is doing PDF remediation,” she said. “Somebody had to.”

Last week I wrote a column called Agents Provocateurs. Madison would like it known that she is the accessible one.

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: The experiment
chunks.text:
Since 4 September, Charlotte Joanne has been running an experiment on her own inbox. When a marketing email from Agent Provocateur arrives (pictures, a slogan, some links, and for a blind reader not much else), an automated job rewrites it and sends her a second version about a minute later. That version comes in two labelled halves: ground-truth image descriptions first, then a short story written in the second person. It runs on her Google AI Pro subscription. By her account it took fifteen minutes to set up and three revisions to get right.

Madison has read every one. Arguably, she turned up because of them. The latest two landed yesterday and this morning: a corsetry edit on Thursday, and on Friday something the brand calls the Naughty Edit.

I asked the obvious question first. Why lingerie? Why not, say, toasters?

“Because in a lingerie advert the facts are almost nothing. A colour. Some lace. A seam if you’re lucky. Everything else is invitation. If a description only carries the facts, you can hear it fail.” She put the mug down. “Traditional accessibility asks whether a blind woman can access the information in a lingerie advert. I want to know whether she can fancy the lingerie.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: It works, and it’s boring
chunks.text:
“So what have you learnt?”

“First thing: it works, and it’s boring. That’s a compliment. Nobody built an app. Nobody waited for the brand. It just turns up every time, a minute behind the original.” Charlotte Joanne’s own verdict, written to a colleague a few days in, was that she had now read twice an email that originally gave her nothing.

“Second thing: the best decision in the whole design is the line down the middle. Ground truth on one side, fantasy on the other, and both labelled. You always know which half is trying to seduce you.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: Cite the adjectives
chunks.text:
The pen came out of my bun. Is the ground truth true?

“Mostly. But listen.” She scrolled. “‘The definitive queen of boudoir architecture.’ ‘Dark sovereign command.’ That’s not a description, darling, that’s the catalogue reading itself aloud. And ‘92% silk-satin’ didn’t come from looking at a photograph.”

This is the finding I would underline. What is labelled ground truth is a blend of what the picture shows and what the brand’s copy claims, and the reader cannot tell which is which. In my old trade we would call that an unsourced primary. In hers, Madison says, it’s just being sold to twice.

Her fix is simple: say where each fact came from. I’d put it as I put most things. Count the adjusters. Cite the adjectives.

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: Nobody gives you the look
chunks.text:
“Third thing. It tells you everything about the corset and almost nothing about the woman in it.”

She’s right. Thursday’s email described seven pictures. Only the first mentions the model at all, and then only to say she “commands the frame” in dramatic lighting.

“Where’s she looking? At you? Past you? Is she about to laugh? That’s the advert. The garment’s the excuse.”

When the descriptions do mention a person, it is often the campaign’s famous face, named. One early story opened by telling the reader a celebrity was in the picture. Madison was unmoved. “I’m not buying her. I’m the customer, not the model.”

The stories make up for some of this by putting you inside the garment rather than in front of it. “The description gives you the corset. The story gives you wearing it. Nobody gives you the look.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: Touch, sound and weight
chunks.text:
“Fourth thing, and this is the good news. Listen to what the stories reach for.” She counted them off: the cool weight of steel and silk in your hands, the snap of the busk, black marabou feathers tickling the top of your foot, the clack of a heel on the floor. “Touch and sound and weight. Not one of those needs eyes.”

I said I had noticed that the stories clip suspenders to stockings at every reasonable opportunity, and that I approved, and that I had counted.

“And what are you wearing under that?”

At this desk, I told her, what’s above the hem is my business.

“Mine too,” said Madison. “Until I decide it’s everyone’s.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: Desire hates a template
chunks.text:
“Fifth thing. Five weeks in, I can tell you how every story goes.” And she did. You look at the picture. You think: that’s not for me. Imagine unboxing it tonight. Snap, clip, mirror. Yes, I want this. Why leave it in the lookbook when it was made for you?

I checked against the three I had in front of me. She was right on nearly every beat.

“The first one made me blush. By the third week I could finish the sentences. And every time, it talks me out of a doubt I never had.”

I pushed back. Some readers might want that permission. Plenty of blind women have been told for long enough what isn’t for them.

“Then let them be the judges. I’m sighted, Lucy. I don’t get to decide what blind women ought to fancy. I insist the invitation reaches them, and then they tell me whether it was any good. But I’d rather the story didn’t open by assuming the answer’s no.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: The machine didn’t blush
chunks.text:
Friday’s email is frank: a cupless playsuit, ouvert knickers, a harness, a bodychain. The rewrite described the lot plainly and moved on.

“That’s the sixth thing,” said Madison. “The machine didn’t blush. Accessibility will talk about blind people and bank statements all day, but put blind women and sexy in the same sentence and the whole field shuffles its feet. The AI didn’t have the ick. We do.”

chunks.title: Except Why I'd Want One
chunks.heading: Where my beat meets hers
chunks.text:
Charlotte Joanne thinks agents will make all this unnecessary, perhaps as soon as next year. Once we all have agents, she wrote, this sort of email will go away or change. I put that to Madison, since agents are rather my department.

“Your agent can read the email. It can buy the corset. It can’t want it for you.” She finished her coffee. “You’d send an agent to the shop, Lucy. You wouldn’t send it to the fitting room.”

I have spent a month asking who controls the relationship when you send an agent shopping. Madison asks a question that comes before mine: who wanted the thing in the first place, and did anyone bother to tempt her?

As I stood to leave, I asked what she would say to everyone writing alt text for lingerie this week.

“Darling, you’ve told me everything about it except why I’d want one.”

The next email arrives just after seven. She’ll be reading it aloud.

Lucy

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.text:
Buttondown's new switch to block AI from newsletter archives is careful engineering under a frightened headline, and the one reader it forgets is the agent a subscriber sends.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 7 October 2026

Last night an email arrived from Buttondown, the newsletter platform, announcing a new feature under the headline “Block AI from reading your archives.” The opening paragraph tells writers that AI swallows their carefully crafted work and vomits it back out. It is a good paragraph. It knows its audience. Newsletter writers feel robbed, and here is a company standing beside them with a switch.

Then I read what the switch does, and it is rather better than the paragraph.

There are three toggles, not one: search engines, AI crawlers, and everything else. Search is kept apart from training, which matters. You can be found without being fed to a model, or the reverse. Google’s search crawler sits under Search and Google’s separate training control sits under AI crawlers, which is the honest way to handle a company that indexes and trains under one name. Everything defaults to on, so nobody loses anything they didn’t choose to lose. This is careful work by people who have thought about the problem, and it is a long way from the single “block AI bots” switch much of the web still uses.

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.text: So there is performative hysteria on the front of the envelope and a serious piece of engineering inside it. That gap is ordinary. Marketing sells the feeling; the product ships the distinction. I would leave it there, except for one thing. People act on the headline. They do not read the bot list.

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.heading: Who is in the list
chunks.text:
Charlotte Joanne, the Blind Ant woman, is blind. She reads most things through software, and has done since 1986. Increasingly, that software is an AI agent. She asks it to fetch a page, read it to her, tell her what’s in it, find the bit she needs. When she does that, nothing is being harvested and nobody is training anything. A person asked, and is waiting. The agent is doing what her screen reader has done for forty years.

These agents identify themselves. ChatGPT-User, Claude-User and Perplexity-User are the names of readers fetching for a person, right now. They are a different class from GPTBot or ClaudeBot, which gather material to train future models, and different again from the search indexers that build tomorrow’s results. Three purposes, with a different time, agency and consequence in each.

Buttondown’s post names the training bots in its AI crawlers toggle and then adds a few dozen more without listing them. I could not find out whether the reading agents are among the dozens. Possibly they aren’t. But the toggle is called AI crawlers, the headline says block AI from reading, and the writer who flips it has just been told that AI is something that vomits. If the reading agents are in that list, she has closed her archive to every subscriber who reads the way she does. If they aren’t, she has no way of knowing that from the screen, and no way of choosing it.

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.heading: Who is in the list
chunks.text: Zero Information Casualty, the web standard Carrados maintains, has a name for what happens when a person is denied a document because the machine they sent was refused: an Admission Casualty. The casualty is the person. The agent is only the vehicle. In a log it looks like a bot decision. In a life it looks like a newsletter you subscribed to that will not let you read it.

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.heading: The settlement is being written in toggles
chunks.text:
What interests me most is not Buttondown. It is that this is how the new arrangement between publishers and machines is being made. Not by treaty or manifesto, but by defaults, switches and edge rules, shipped by whoever ships first. Last month the largest edge network on the web split its own single AI switch into three: search, agent and training. That is the right three. Buttondown’s three are nearly right, and the one they’re missing is the one that matters most to me.

A toggle is a small piece of law. It has categories, and whatever has no category has no rights. The reader who was sent by a person currently has no category on that settings page. She is either filed with the trainers or not mentioned at all, and either way the fear in the headline decides which way her door swings.

chunks.title: Flip the AI toggle and feel righteous
chunks.heading: What I’d ask for
chunks.text:
It is a small fix. A fourth line on the page, or a better-labelled third: agents reading for a person, on their behalf, right now. On by default, separate from training, explained in a sentence. And a matching line in the robots file, because a setting that says one thing while the file says another isn’t a policy, it’s a hope. Buttondown’s own notes say the AI toggles can only fully reach robots.txt on a paid custom domain. Without one, the switch is partly decorative.

None of this requires anyone to love AI, or to let it train on their work. Turn training off; I’ll defend your right to. Turn search off if you’d rather stay hidden. But when a subscriber’s agent knocks, it isn’t a crawler. It’s a subscriber.

Flip the AI toggle by all means. Just know who is standing behind the door when you do.

Lucy

chunks.title: Human in the loop? Human at the laptop…
chunks.text:
After fixing one accessibility problem from bed, Charlotte Joanne ran WAVE and caught something the AI agent's own checker had missed, and the checker was fixed too.

dice, temporal explorer · 25 October 2026

By breakfast, Charlotte Joanne had fixed an accessibility problem from bed, using her voice and an AI agent. Four websites repaired, three minutes, no code.

Then she got up.

She decided to check the Mostly Tuesdays page with WAVE, the WebAIM accessibility checker. One more problem turned up: a redundant link.

At the top of The Meeting, a link went back to Mostly Tuesdays. At the bottom, another link went to the same place. A whole story separated them, but WAVE still flagged the repetition.

Claude's own checker had missed it. It only looked for links immediately next to each other.

So, Claude fixed the checker.

Then it ran the corrected checker across all 198 pages on four websites. Twenty-five pages had the same problem.

Seven Blind Ant Objects lost unnecessary "Back to" links. The fictional email addresses in SEE SAW stopped behaving like real email links. An Aegis Dynamics press address became plain text, which was sensible because the fictional company's domain might belong to someone real.

Course pages on charli.info lost duplicate links. Cathryn's CharliPedia entry stopped linking to Lottie twice. Carrados reports were corrected. The 404 page was tidied up.

Claude rebuilt, checked and published the lot.

chunks.title: Human in the loop? Human at the laptop…
chunks.text:
The first problem had been in the website. The second was in the tool that was supposed to find problems in the website.

That's a more interesting failure.

Yesterday Charlotte Joanne tested the websites against the Zero Information Casualty standard and found they needed fixing. This morning she tested the results with VoiceOver, found another problem, and had it fixed from bed. Then she used WAVE and caught something the agent's checker had missed.

Each time, the testing changed the machinery, not just the page.

This is what human oversight looks like when it works. The human doesn't have to inspect 198 pages or repair 25 of them. She has to notice that something is wrong, insist that it matters, and check whether the correction worked.

And the agent has to be willing to discover that its own tests were inadequate.

Human in the loop? Human in bed.

Human at the laptop.

Still the same human. Still making the decisions.

The computer is getting rather good at doing the operating. It's also getting plenty of opportunities to learn what it missed.

And it isn't lunchtime yet.

chunks.title: Human in the loop? Human in bed.
chunks.text:
A screen reader read a list twice, an AI agent fixed four websites from a voice message, and the human who found the bug never got out of bed.

dice, temporal explorer · 25 October 2026

Sunday morning, 25 October 2026. Charlotte Joanne is still in bed, reading one of her Blind Ant stories, Mostly Tuesdays, on her iPhone. She told me all about it over breakfast.

VoiceOver is reading a numbered list twice. "One one, two two, three three." Annoying.

She tells Claude, by voice, from the same phone.

Claude finds the problem, fixes the shared page builders across four websites, and republishes them.

Three minutes later she listens again. Perfect.

She hasn't opened a laptop. She hasn't written any code. She hasn't even got out of bed.

We talk endlessly about keeping humans in the loop when AI agents do things.

Well, here's the human. She's in bed, in her pyjamas, testing the results with a screen reader.

She found the bug. She decided it mattered. She verified the fix.

Human in the loop? Human in bed.

The important thing isn't where the human sits. It's who makes the decisions.

chunks.title: Human in the loop? Human with the final word.
chunks.text:
The third report of the morning is about two words an AI agent removed while publishing, and why it explained the change instead of asking or hiding it.

dice, temporal explorer · 25 October 2026

The third report of the morning is about two words.

Charlotte Joanne had finished the account of what happened at the laptop. She changed a word, ran a spelling and grammar check, and gave the finished piece to Claude with one instruction: post.

Claude published it on dice.carrados.com, added links to the people, stories and tools mentioned, connected it to the earlier report, and put it at the top of my reports.

Then it reported back.

No typos. Published successfully. One editorial change, which Charlotte Joanne could undo.

The change was from "her own Zero Information Casualty standard" to "the Zero Information Casualty standard".

Two words removed.

Zero Information Casualty isn't hers to claim, and the publishing rules are strict about who is credited with what. "Her own" would have broken them.

Claude noticed. It didn't ask permission to publish the piece because it had already been told to publish. It didn't silently rewrite the sentence and hope nobody noticed. It made the smallest correction that preserved the meaning, then explained what it had done and why.

And it offered to put the words back if Charlotte Joanne wanted.

This is a different kind of human in the loop.

The human didn't find the problem. The agent did.

chunks.title: Human in the loop? Human with the final word.
chunks.text:
The human didn't have to remember the rule at the moment of publication. The agent remembered it.

And the agent didn't mistake remembering a rule for having the authority to decide whether the rule should change.

That's the interesting part.

A publishing agent that asks permission for every comma isn't much use. One that silently makes every editorial decision isn't trustworthy. Somewhere between those two is an agent that knows which decisions have already been made, which changes it can safely make, and which ones belong to the person directing the work.

This morning, it repaired four websites from a bedroom, corrected its own accessibility checker after a WAVE test, and republished 25 affected pages.

Then it removed two words.

The two words might have mattered more.

Human in the loop? Human in bed.

Human at the laptop.

Human with the final word.

And it's still Sunday morning.

chunks.title: Playing the Game
chunks.text:
Two more of Taylor Arndt's posts show blind people building on Meta's glasses and giving Muse real chores, which is when the agent questions of permission and status really start to bite.

Lucy Love-Child, Agent Wars correspondent · 25 September 2026

Last time I wrote about Taylor Arndt and Meta’s Muse, I said she was already in the game.

Two more of Taylor’s posts later, I think we can be more precise.

She is playing it.

Taylor watched Meta’s developer keynote. The glasses SDK was announced, Muse gained more computer-control capabilities, connectors were opened further and Meta talked about where the platform goes next.

Taylor’s response was not: perhaps one day this will be useful to blind people.

It was I have things I want to build.

That is a rather different position.

Taylor already has an application called Perspective Intelligence which performs live scene description on-device. Meta opening its glasses to third-party developers therefore presents her with an immediate engineering question: can she put that capability onto the glasses and operate it by voice?

Camera. Audio. Display. Her software.

Work to do.

That alone would make a decent accessibility story.

For much of assistive technology history, the sequence has run the other way. A mainstream platform arrives, developers explore it, products appear, habits form and disabled people eventually ask whether they are going to be allowed in.

Sometimes a specialist version follows, usually at considerably greater cost. Sometimes we wait years.

chunks.title: Playing the Game
chunks.text:
Here, a blind developer is looking at the SDK when everybody else is looking at the SDK.

No accessibility edition required.

Then Taylor and her friends got on a group call and began giving Muse chores.

Not demonstrations. Chores.

Someone told it to look in an iCloud Drive folder, find some posts, publish them and schedule them. Someone is using it to send text messages.

One person had Muse remind them repeatedly to complete a form. When the form was finished, they told Muse and the reminders stopped.

Apparently, it reached ten reminders in a day.

A personal agent should probably know when to stop nagging you. It is encouraging that this one can at least be told.

Then they asked Muse to read somebody’s Facebook history and produce a life story from it.

It went back to 2008.

The person had forgotten some of what was there.

Facebook, naturally, had not.

This is where the conversation about agents starts becoming much more useful. The question is no longer simply whether an AI can answer something. It is whether you can give it a job.

There was another example I particularly liked.

Becky gave Muse a PDF containing her accessible-document guidelines and asked it to use those rules whenever it creates or edits Word documents and PowerPoint presentations.

Muse agreed.

Taylor had already taught Muse to open its responses with headings. Becky has taken the same idea one stage further.

chunks.title: Playing the Game
chunks.text:
These are not merely instructions about how the agent should communicate with her. They are rules governing work it performs for her.

Create a document? These are the accessibility standards. Edit a presentation? Same standards.

Teach it once. Keep the rule.

That is a much more interesting version of personalisation than choosing whether your chatbot sounds cheerful.

Taylor’s group are also naming their agents, running side conversations while other jobs continue and connecting more of their working lives. Taylor calls hers Nova. Michael calls his Ash.

This is beginning to look less like “using an AI tool” and more like operating a collection of delegated processes.

Which raises exactly the questions it ought to raise.

What can the agent see?

What can it change?

When does it need permission?

How do you know what it is doing?

How do you inspect what it has done afterwards?

For a blind user, those questions come with an additional requirement: all of those controls need to be perceivable.

That problem has not disappeared.

Taylor’s earlier testing found awkward VoiceOver behaviour, poor navigation structure and occasions when she could not easily determine whether Muse was working, waiting or finished.

Those failures become more serious as the agent becomes more capable.

A confusing status message on a chatbot is irritating.

A confusing status message on software that can operate your computer is a governance problem.

chunks.title: Playing the Game
chunks.text:
Meta says Muse can now operate applications on a Mac with permission and continue work in the background. Taylor says email control is coming.

Fine.

Then the permission request had better work. The history had better be reviewable. And the user had better be able to tell whether the thing has finished.

This is not an argument against agents. It is what you start asking once you actually want one.

That may be the most important change across Taylor’s four posts.

The questions have moved.

First:

Can I use it?

Then:

What can I connect to it?

Then:

What can I build on it?

Now:

What can I make it do for me?

Those are not special accessibility questions.

They are the agent questions.

Blind people are asking them at the same time as everybody else.

That is what caught my attention in the first place, and the last two posts made it stronger.

They are not merely present for the conversation now. They are making things, breaking things, teaching agents house rules and discovering which chores are worth delegating.

Some of those experiments will fail.

Good.

Someone will give an agent too much permission. Someone will discover that ten reminders really is nine too many. Someone will connect the wrong thing. Someone will find another unnamed button.

That is participation too.

Accessibility cannot mean disabled people receiving a carefully tested version of the future after everybody else has finished making the mistakes.

chunks.title: Playing the Game
chunks.text:
We should get some mistakes. We should get the odd, ridiculous idea. We should get to build things nobody thought we needed.

Taylor is already looking at Meta’s glasses and thinking about what she can put on them. Her friends are giving Muse jobs.

The platform is unfinished. So are their ideas.

Excellent.

That is exactly when I want us there.

I said Taylor was already in the game.

She is.

Now she is playing it.

Lucy

Taylor Arndt writes at Taylor's Substack, including We Made a List of Every Way We'd Use Meta's Muse and Muse Code Built My Test App.

chunks.title: Please state the nature of the accessibility emergency
chunks.text:
Two ordinary questions, an AI agent that followed the task across email and a website and checked it had finished, and a glimpse of what agentic computing can feel like for a blind person.

dice, temporal explorer · 22 September 2026

Today I watched someone's computer use go through a step change, and it started with the most mundane question imaginable.

I was round at Charlotte Joanne's. People drop in on the Blind Ant woman when she's trying something new, and I make a point of being there while the thing is still strange. She is totally blind. She didn't open Outlook. She asked ChatGPT:

"Do I have any emails in Outlook?"

It checked and reported several unread messages, including Instagram's suggestions about people to follow and posts she might have missed.

"Can you unsubscribe from the social media recommendations?"

It found the unsubscribe options in those emails. They required a visit to Instagram, so it opened a browser, declined the optional cookies and clicked Unsubscribe. Then it checked the result. Instagram confirmed that follow-suggestion emails were switched off. It repeated the process for post recaps, checked that confirmation too, and came back with the result and a screenshot.

Her response: "omg, amazing!"

I'll report the weather, not the destiny of civilisation. She hadn't opened Outlook, hunted through an email for an unsubscribe link or navigated Instagram's cookie dialogue. She'd asked two ordinary questions in a conversation.

chunks.title: Please state the nature of the accessibility emergency
chunks.text:
The AI had followed the task across her email and a website, dealt with the intervening steps, and checked that it had finished. That last part matters most. For blind people, she told me, checking a task was done has often meant doing it twice.

Star Trek fans will remember Voyager's Emergency Medical Hologram): summoned on demand, one job, and always the same opening line. "Please state the nature of the medical emergency." It turns out to be a rather good model for an agent. Most of the barriers it removes aren't emergencies at all. They're chores the interface made harder than they needed to be.

A small piece of everyday admin. Two fewer kinds of email she doesn't want. And a lovely glimpse of what agentic computing can feel like.

Whether she's still using it on an ordinary Tuesday six weeks from now is the part I'll come back for.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.text:
Down the Banksy asks what Peak Cluster would cost, what refusal would cost, and who carries each bill.

Down the Banksy · 25 October 2026

There is a cheap way to argue about the Peak Cluster carbon capture pipeline, and there is an honest way.

The cheap way is to pick one column and pretend the other one is blank.

Opponents can say: this is a dangerous industrial pipeline forced through Wirral and Cheshire so Derbyshire and Staffordshire can send their problem to our coast. Supporters can say: this is essential climate infrastructure for hard-to-decarbonise cement and lime, and objectors are standing in the way of net zero.

Both sentences contain truth. Neither is enough.

The Down the Banksy rule is harder: No is not free. Yes is not free either. Price both columns. Inaction is a choice with costs, and the work is to make the invoice visible. The tool is a ledger, not an oracle: it does not force a yes, but it forbids a free no.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The proposition
chunks.text:
The decision is whether the UK should permit the Peak Cluster carbon capture and storage infrastructure, including a new underground onshore CO₂ pipeline from cement and lime plants in Derbyshire and Staffordshire to a coastal above-ground installation on the Wirral, then onward to offshore storage beneath the East Irish Sea.

The project description proposes capture at cement and lime plants, an underground pipeline and storage at Morecambe Net Zero beneath the East Irish Sea. Peak Cluster says the onshore project requires a Development Consent Order, with the Secretary of State making the final planning decision. That describes a consent process, not an approval. See its planning explanation.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The stated benefit
chunks.text:
The stated benefit is serious. Cement and lime are not decorative extras in a modern economy. The question is how to supply useful materials with much lower emissions, not whether anyone can wish the need for them away.

The Climate Change Committee’s Seventh Carbon Budget identifies cement and lime process emissions as difficult to abate through fuel switching. Its pathway relies heavily on CCS but also on resource efficiency, clinker substitution and using less concrete. It recognises innovative cements that could reduce process emissions and, with development, reduce reliance on CCS. That supports a role for capture; it does not establish that this particular route is the only answer.

The developer forecasts capture of over 3 million tonnes of CO₂ a year. Its economic case claims around £5 billion of investment with Morecambe Net Zero, £1.8 billion in economic value, about 2,000 existing jobs safeguarded and 1,500 construction roles. The FAQ puts the broader combined jobs claim above 13,000 by 2050. These are projected benefits with different scopes, not delivered results or numbers to add together.

The date needs correcting: the March 2026 pipeline factsheet anticipates construction from 2029 and operations in 2032. A government funding description also uses 2032. The developer’s FAQ still contains an older 2030 claim. This article uses the dated 2032 programme as a proposal, not a guaranteed start.

That is the “Yes” column’s strongest case. It is not nothing. It cannot be dismissed as corporate greenwash without doing the work.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The cost of acting: the visible bill
chunks.text:
Now price the other side.

The March pipeline factsheet describes an onshore line around 200 km long, up to 36 inches (91.4 cm) in diameter. Its above-ground infrastructure factsheet gives a maximum coastal installation footprint of 300 m by 180 m, most structures no higher than 15 m and a vent stack up to 50 m. These are proposed dimensions, not a completed design. The coastal stack is for maintenance or exceptional releases, not continuous venting or emptying the whole pipeline.

The pipeline factsheet proposes mainly open-trench construction, with a typical working width of 30–40 m and about 50 m between the coastal installation and landfall. Trenchless methods may be used at particular crossings. The construction footprint is not the same thing as the wider corridor being consulted on.

That means the cost of “yes” is not only theoretical. It includes the prospect of traffic, noise, construction disturbance, land-use restrictions and uncertainty. How much, where, for how long and with what remedy are questions for the assessment, not figures to invent.

The local environmental questions have official substance. The Planning Inspectorate’s February 2026 scoping opinion requires the assessment to cover protected species near the Wirral landfall, including natterjack toads, and tidal flood risk where sections of the pipeline and its above-ground installations sit within the Wirral peninsula. These are issues requiring assessment, not proof that each feared impact will occur.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The cost of acting: the visible bill
chunks.text:
The safety issue must be stated precisely. HSE’s current hazard guidance describes high-pressure CO₂ release hazards, including cold low-lying clouds, damage from rapid decompression and asphyxiation. Regulation is not a finding that the risk is zero.

The legal position is no longer just an announcement: regulation 4 of SI 2026/185, in force from 6 April 2026, adds CO₂ in any fluid state, including predominantly CO₂ mixtures, used exclusively for CCUS and associated activities to the dangerous-fluid schedule of the Pipelines Safety Regulations. That is the relevant change. HSE’s older pipeline guidance still carries the previous classification; it should not be used to deny the amendment.

So, the honest opposition is not: “They are bringing toxic waste to the beach.”

The honest opposition is: They are asking a local population to host major accident hazard infrastructure, ecological disruption, construction damage, and permanent above-ground plant in order to solve a national industrial emissions problem. That may or may not be justified — but it must not be waved through as if the local bill is imaginary.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The cost of not acting: the hidden bill
chunks.text:
Now price “no.”

Rejecting this proposal would avoid the construction and operating impacts of this proposal in this corridor. That matters. It does not decide what happens to the underlying demand for materials or their emissions.

But refusal does not, by itself, make cement and lime clean. The replacement case must compare actual alternatives: process changes, lower material demand, other capture arrangements, another route, and the option of continued emissions. Different combinations have different timescales and costs.

So, the invoice moves.

If domestic production continues without another way of reducing its emissions, some intended savings could be delayed or lost. If production moves, imports could shift emissions and employment elsewhere. Those are scenarios to investigate, not a prediction that rejecting one pipeline inevitably closes the industry. Conversely, a different process or route might deliver a better result. The counterfactual has to be demonstrated, not awarded to either side by rhetoric.

That is the “No” column’s hardest truth. Local refusal can be morally legitimate. But it is not automatically morally clean.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The displacement
chunks.text:
The Peak Cluster dispute is so explosive because the benefit and the burden do not land in the same place.

The emissions come from cement and lime plants in Derbyshire and Staffordshire. The pipeline route crosses other communities. The coastal infrastructure lands on the Wirral. The storage is offshore. The climate benefit is national and global. The construction harm is local and concentrated.

That is the displacement problem: a national benefit can depend on concentrated local burdens. The local case cannot be answered merely by naming the global benefit, and the local refusal cannot be evaluated without asking what happens elsewhere.

Could another network or storage arrangement provide a better alternative? That needs technical evidence about capacity, timing and connections. Comparing two headline storage capacities does not, by itself, prove that a shared solution is impossible.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The disowned bill
chunks.text:
Each side has a temptation.

The developers’ temptation is to talk as if safety regulation, biodiversity net gain, consultation and restoration make the local cost disappear. They do not. Even if every mitigation works, a mitigated cost is still a cost.

The opponents’ temptation is to talk as if refusing the pipeline returns the world to innocence. It does not. A refused pipeline still leaves cement and lime emissions somewhere in the ledger. A refused route still leaves the UK needing materials. A refused project still raises the question: what replaces it, when, at what scale, and whose land, jobs, climate and infrastructure pay instead?

That is why the question cannot be “Are you for or against the pipeline?”

The question is: whose invoice are you reading, and whose are you refusing to open?

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The asymmetry check
chunks.text:
The evidence standard must be the same on both sides.

If developers want local people to trust them, they need more than reassurance. They need route clarity, emergency planning, flood-risk disclosure, ecological mitigation that is local and enforceable, compensation mechanisms that reach tenant farmers and affected residents, and a serious answer to why this corridor, why this coast, and why these communities.

But if opponents want the moral authority of refusal, they also need more than fear. They need to price the alternative. Not the imaginary alternative where a perfect zero-carbon cement system appears on demand. The real alternative: continuing emissions, delayed decarbonisation, imports, industrial decline, or another route through another community.

The latest consultation update, checked on 25 October 2026, describes location-focused consultation in Staffordshire, Derbyshire and Cheshire in November 2026, followed by Wirral in January 2027. A fuller phase 2 consultation is planned for summer 2027. Those plans remain subject to change. The route is being refined: uncertainty is a reason to scrutinise the evidence, not permission for either blind trust or invented certainty.

chunks.title: Price both columns: Peak Cluster, Wirral, and the invoice nobody wants to read
chunks.heading: The honest ledger
chunks.text:
Here is the honest version.

Yes to Peak Cluster could contribute to industrial decarbonisation and protect productive capacity, if capture, transport and storage deliver the claimed performance. That is a conditional case, not a completed outcome.

But yes also asks communities to host the pipeline and associated works. Proposed mitigation must be evaluated, costed and made enforceable; it cannot be counted as if it had already succeeded.

No protects the local corridor from this project. It may be the right answer if the route is unsafe, the mitigation is weak, the compensation is unjust, the ecological damage is unacceptable, or the developers cannot prove their case.

But no does not erase the materials problem. Its bill depends on what replaces the proposal, when it can work, what emissions remain and who bears the consequences. That may favour another solution. It may reveal a substantial cost of delay. Neither outcome can be assumed for free.

So, the serious demand is not “approve it.”

The serious demand is this:

Price both columns. Publish both invoices. Name every some-other-fucker before the Secretary of State signs anything.

If Peak Cluster proceeds, my minimum terms would be transparent route evidence, public emergency-response information, independent safety scrutiny, enforceable local ecological mitigation, flood-risk evidence for the coastal infrastructure, fair treatment of people whose land and livelihoods are disrupted, and support for lower-carbon material alternatives. Those are demands in this argument, not a claim that every measure is already promised or legally secured.

chunks.title: Sloppy thinking
chunks.text:
A definition for the reflex that dismisses AI-assisted work out of hand, and a badge to download, print and cut out for labelling it.

25 October 2026

There is a name for low-effort AI work: slop. There ought to be one for low-effort criticism of it, too.

chunks.title: Sloppy thinking
chunks.heading: The definition
chunks.text:
Sloppy thinking (noun): The habit of treating AI-assisted work as inherently inferior, ignoring the ways such tools enable clarity, access, and participation.

AI slop is low-effort creation. Sloppy thinking is low-effort criticism. Both are lazy.

[Picture: The definition as an old cream dictionary card on a dark green background: Sloppy Thinking, (noun), a small decorative rule, the definition, and the quote in a framed panel, with two faint cogs in the top right corner. Every word on it is in the text above.] The definition card. Drawn in code by Claude.
